item.description: Biomedical research is constrained by the time and domain expertise required to analyze increasingly large and complex datasets. Here we present OpenScientist, an open-source agentic AI co-scientist designed to address this gap by investigating scientist-defined queries and generating verifiable, data-grounded analyses. OpenScientist was evaluated by domain experts across five biomedical case studies, completing analyses in minutes that otherwise would take months of human time and expertise. It accurately quantified Alzheimer’s blood biomarker performance, generated a plasma proteomic survival model that predicted survival in a hidden-evaluation cohort, proposed a reproducible mechanism linking tau pathology to altered lysosomal acidification, generated multiple myeloma hypotheses validated in an external cohort with attenuated signal in randomized controls, and demonstrated concordance with an independent human analysis in a blinded, prespecified proteomic comparison. These results support the use of OpenScientist to assist biomedical data analysis in concert with human experts. item.description: Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging1–4, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an ‘add-on’ architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. item.title: 【Self-driving laboratories】 Filter By:
item.description: Antimicrobial resistance is among the most pressing healthcare challenges of our time. Multidrug-resistant ‘superbugs’ continue to emerge at an alarming rate, while antibiotic development has stalled in recent decades. Antimicrobial peptides have attracted interest for their potent bactericidal activity and lower propensity to spur resistance; however, translation into clinical practice has been hampered by poor bioavailability, challenging syntheses and limited stability. By contrast, synthetic copolymers mimicking antimicrobial peptides have received attention for their efficacy and synthetic tractability. Here we highlight recent advances in antimicrobial polymer development and discuss future directions for their design and implementation. We also outline future research directions, including the use of machine learning to guide polymer design and the development of scalable production methods that ensure the worldwide accessibility of these materials. Antimicrobial polymers offer an attractive tool for combating the crisis of antimicrobial resistance.
